title: Here Begins the Section on Performance
summary: Opens the performance section: as metre makes speech pleasing, tāla makes rāga so. Pathak ji contrasts bound and unbound singing, shows how timing changes meaning, matches bānsurī tonguing syllables to sitar and tabla bols, separates gat from song, lists kinds of singing, gives rules for syllable length, and defines sam.

prev.title: Rāga Vṛndāvanī Sāraṅg, Layālāp and Free Tānas

blocks.text: Now begins the Pradarśana Prakaraṇa (chapter on performance)
Pradarśana Khaṇḍa (performance section)

blocks.verse:
छन्दों बद्धो यथा वाक्यः सर्वस्मै रोचते खलु।
ताले बद्धस्तथा रागों गायकस्य धनं महत्।१२९।
blocks.text: Just as a sentence bound in metre pleases everyone, so a rāga bound in tāla is the singer's great wealth.

That is, when a sentence is endowed with qualities such as figures of speech (alaṅkāra), it is called prose poetry (gadya kāvya), which pleases only poets. But when that same sentence is bound into a beautiful chanda (metre), it becomes pleasing to all people. These two kinds can be seen in all things of the world: loose tea and packed tea, loose cloth and stitched clothes, plain talk and talk steeped in rasa (aesthetic flavour), a naked creature and a creature clothed, and so on. In every field each has its own importance. The essence of this is that -

blocks.verse:
बद्धाय जीवाय निबद्धगानम् मुक्ताय जीवाय विमुक्त गानम्।
अद्वैत भावेन विमुक्त गानम् द्वैत प्रघानं तु निबद्ध गानम्।१३०।
blocks.text: For the bound soul, bound singing; for the free soul, free singing. Free singing comes from a sense of non-duality; bound singing is ruled by duality.

Although there is no being in this world who is completely free, still some are more bound and some less. So the free being prefers free singing (mukta gāna) and open places, and bound beings prefer nibaddha gāna (bound, metred singing) and well-enclosed places.

Just as a thing is tied up securely when it is moved from one place to another, so the singer's rāga, which in the form of ālāpa was 'svāntaḥ sukhāya' (for one's own inner joy), is now going to be bound in tāla for 'parānta sukhāya' (for the joy of others). So bound music cannot be carried on without two persons. These two kinds are usually as much in dispute as the doctrines of non-duality (advaitavāda) and duality (dvaitavāda). To be free of these disputes, adopting the baṛā khayāl as a reconciling view (sāmyavāda) would suit the age. That is why khayāl singing is more widespread than dhrupad singing, for too much bondage (bandhan) is held to be a cause of wailing (krandan).

blocks.verse:
न्यूनाधिक्येन कालस्य वाक्यार्थः परिवर्त्यते।
ताल काल प्रभावेन राग भावो विशिष्यते।१३१।
blocks.text: By lessening or lengthening time, the meaning of a sentence is changed; by the power of tāla and time, the feeling of a rāga is made distinct.

That is, in the world of music, for the expression of feeling, laya (tempo) and tāla (metric cycle) have an important place along with rāga. Just as various chandas (metres) are described in the world of literature, so many kinds of tāla are described in music. If the number of mātrās (beats) and a particular order of short and long [syllables] give birth to a metre, then the number of mātrās and a particular division of the mātrās create a tāla.

This is why Tāla Dhamār, Tāla Dīpcandī and Āḍā Cārtāl, though all are tālas of the same number of mātrās (beats), have their own separate existence because of differences in the division of the mātrās. To know clearly the importance of tāla in rāga, a few sentences are offered. For example: (1) roko mat, jāne do [don't stop (him), let (him) go]. roko, mat jāne do [stop (him), don't let (him) go]. (2) jā, pānī lā [go, bring water]. jāpānī lā [bring the Japanese one]. (3) surāhī banā [make a water-jar]. surā hī banā [make only liquor]. su rāhī banā [become a good traveller]. In these sentences time is the cause of the change of meaning; so it is easy to understand and to explain the sense of tāla on the basis of words. In stringed instruments (tantu vādya), the responsibility of making clear the sense of tāla and laya (tempo) is given to the right hand. For it is said (śrutir mātā layaḥ pitā - śruti is the mother, laya the father) (the mother's place being on the left side and the father's on the right is also a symbol of Indian tradition.) But in wind instruments (suṣira vādya) like the bansī (bamboo bānsurī), both hands are taken up by the notes alone. So the tongue alone has to represent laya, tāla and words. Sitar players make many words from dā and rā, e.g. - dā dir dā rā, dir dā dir dā, dā radā –ra dā. In the same way bansī players imagine various words from ṭa and ka, e.g. - ṭā ṭak ṭā kā, ṭakṭak ṭā kā ṭā kaṭā –ka ṭā, and so on; with such rhythm-showing words they can follow the sitar. If one wishes to translate these symbolic words into meaningful words, a special vocabulary can be formed, e.g. -

ṭa ṭak ṭa kaṭak ṭak ṭa kaandṭa kaṭ –ka ṭabansī (bānsurī)
tā tiṭ tin nātiṭ tiṭ tin nāandtā titā –ti tātabla

blocks.text: In the same way other words too can be translated into the language of instruments. This proves that it must have been metrical poetry of regular timing that gave birth to the tālas. From here it became necessary to show the meeting of literature and music. Sādhakas (learners) should try to count some poems by their mātrās and to write and recite them with the proper tāla. Then they should try to blend them with a rāga; only then will they understand bandiśes (compositions) properly. Although in old texts you will find many bandiśes in which the mātrās of short and long syllables are not kept as they are - in some places a short syllable takes even more mātrās than a long one, and elsewhere a long syllable is given even less time than a short one - such bandiśes can confuse learners. So they should treat those bandiśes as exceptions, and at the beginning, not considering themselves fit for them, attend only to simple bandiśes. Then, gradually becoming able, they will come to know the secret of those bandiśes too. Just as nourishing food is harmful for a patient, so for those of little knowledge a deep subject does not increase knowledge but increases pride. If the grace of the guru (teacher) is not obtained, that same śāstra, instead of making me a sādhaka, can present me as a bādhaka (hindrance). So my one invaluable suggestion for sādhakas is this:

blocks.verse:
कायशौचम् मनः शुद्धिः प्राणः सोधम् समाचरेत्।
जिज्ञासुर्गुरुमाश्रित्य संगीतज्ञः सुखी भवेत्।१३२।
blocks.text: One should practise cleanliness of body, purity of mind and purification of the breath; the seeker who takes refuge in a guru becomes a happy musician.

Having gained cleanliness and health of the body, having washed with the soap of faith the mind soiled by impurities such as attachment and aversion, and then having freed the prāṇa (life-breath) and the mind and intellect from restlessness through prāṇāyāma (breath control) and the like - when the desire to know arises in the mind, only then does one search for a guru (teacher). And only by gaining knowledge from the guru does the musician find happiness and peace. So keep the temple of your mind always lit with the lamp of goodwill and faith; otherwise, like insects and vermin in an empty house, many enemies such as hatred, pride, envy and anger will enter that temple of the mind uninvited. Then, instead of good (artha), only harm (anartha) can come. Then, in that corrupted mind, even separate knowledge of word, rāga and tāla will become impossible. Then the confluence of these three will be as far from them as the confluence at Prayāg is for base people living at that place of pilgrimage: though within reach, it remains out of reach. The subject from here on is somewhat deep, so keep your mind safe from faults and make it pure, so that one may enjoy it properly. In the next śloka the difference between gat and gīt is described.

blocks.verse:
गत गीते समेस्याताम् शब्द मात्रम् विशेषता।
सशब्दं गीतमित्याहुः शब्दहीनं गतम् भवेत्।१३३।
blocks.text: Gat and gīt are alike; the only difference is the words. With words it is called a gīt; without words it is a gat.

That is, the only difference between gat (instrumental composition) and gīt (song) is this: if a sentence or poem with meaningful words is joined with notes and tālas, it is called a gīt, and if the words are taken out of it, that same thing is called a gat. But in composing, it is necessary at the beginning stage to take the help of words. So one should first compose the bandiś in the form of a song and then play it as a gat. In the śāstra of music it is said: first singing, then playing. Playing is held to be a part of singing. In the following śloka the kinds of singing are given.

blocks.verse:
काव्य प्रधानं च रसप्रधानं तालप्रधानं च स्वरप्रधानम्।
नाट्य प्रधानं च निबद्धगानम् भावप्रधानं त्वनिबद्ध गानम्।१३४।
blocks.text: Singing where poetry leads, where rasa leads, where tāla leads, where svara leads and where drama leads is bound singing; singing where bhāva leads is unbound singing.

That is, a song in which the beauty of the poetry is greater and no special attention is paid to rāga and tāla is called kāvya-pradhāna (where poetry leads) singing, such as the Gīta Govinda and the like. Likewise, where the beauty of both poetry and notes together brings out some rasa (aesthetic flavour), as in ṭhumrī, ghazal and so on, it is called rasa-pradhāna (where rasa leads) singing; dhrupad, dhamār and so on are called tāla-pradhāna (where tāla leads), and khayāl svara-pradhāna (where svara leads); ālhā (ballad), nauṭaṅkī and the like, in which attention is kept on a story, are called nāṭya-pradhāna (where drama leads) singing. But singing in which there is no tāla at all, where ālāpa is done only with notes, or with notes helped by a few words, is called bhāva-pradhāna (where bhāva leads) anibaddha gāna (unbound, unmetred singing). So, apart from this, all the kinds above are called nibaddha gāna (bound, metred singing).

For nibaddha gāna (bound singing), it would be proper to practise speaking and writing syllables counted in their natural mātrās (beats). So now attend to the following rules for the natural mātrās of syllables.
A short syllable has one mātrā; a long syllable has two mātrās.
A syllable with anusvāra or visarga, and one that comes before a conjunct, counts as long.

That is, a short syllable is to be taken as of one mātrā and a long syllable as of two mātrās. A syllable with anusvāra or visarga is also to be taken as of two mātrās, and a short syllable that comes before a conjunct letter should also be taken as long, of two mātrās. The method of writing and reading them in music notation is as follows.

blocks.text: In this way the mātrās of words should be counted in their natural form when writing and reading. But in some places, as exceptions, people also sing e, o, ai and au short, e.g. - te re – me – re –. ek rā – t meṃ. hamā – rā ha mā – rā – - and so on. To gain knowledge of these subtle elements of music, contact with a guru, with a pure mind, is necessary. On the basis of the rule above, every caupāī of the Rāmāyaṇa will be of 32 mātrās.
In nibaddha gāna (bound singing) the sam (first beat of the cycle) is of great importance, so we cannot go further without understanding the definition of sam.

blocks.verse:
यत्र रागस्य मुख्यांगम् तालस्यादौ विधीयते।
गुरूवर्णस्य तत्रैव संगमः सम उच्यते।१३५।
blocks.text: Where the main part of the rāga is placed at the start of the tāla, and a long syllable meets it right there, that meeting is called sam.

That is, where on the first mātrā the main part of the rāga and some long syllable of the words come together and, as if from colliding with each other, seem to halt - this confluence of three streams is called sam (first beat of the cycle). For example, in the song "madhuvan meṃ rādhikā nācī re" [Rādhikā danced in Madhuvan], the main part of the words (nā), the main part of the rāga (Dha) and the first mātrā of the tāla - these three meet and it becomes full of rasa. This is the special quality of sam.
